notes: CAC trade union recognition ballot jurisdiction; academic appeal on public law point with concession on irrationality.

enrichment.short_title: Ultraframe v CAC: jurisdiction to investigate recognition ballot irregularities

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: GMB and URTU sought statutory recognition at Ultraframe after a secret ballot fell four votes short of the 40 per cent threshold.
The CAC panel investigated complaints that five members had not received ballot papers, found they would have voted for recognition, and ordered a re-run.
Ultraframe challenged the CAC's jurisdiction and the rationality of the panel's decision in judicial review; Davis J quashed the re-ballot order.
On appeal the CAC conceded irrationality and limited the appeal to a declaration on jurisdiction; the court heard the public law point despite its academicity between the parties.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on judicial review of the Central Arbitration Committee's decision to order a fresh recognition ballot.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; declaration made that the CAC had jurisdiction under the 1992 Act to order a further ballot, but Davis J's quashing order stood because of the conceded irrationality.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 29 of Schedule A1 does not limit the CAC to mechanically accepting a Qualified Independent Person's ballot figures; read with the statutory scheme and the CAC's specialist role, it has supervisory jurisdiction to investigate and annul an invalid ballot before acting on the result.
legal_issues: Whether the CAC's only power after receiving ballot results is to make the paragraph 29 declaration
Whether investigating ballot irregularities after delivery of QIP figures exceeds statutory jurisdiction
Whether the court should decide an academic public law issue on appeal
Whether the CAC panel acted irrationally in ordering a re-ballot
linked_authorities: R (Kwik-Fit (GB) Ltd) v Central Arbitration Committee [2002] ICR 1212
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex p Salem [1999] 1 AC 450

confidence.notes: Jurisdiction reasoning and final declaration are clearly stated; irrationality was conceded and not determined.

notes: Fixed-price waste removal contract construction; appeal dismissed on quantum meruit and variation findings.

enrichment.short_title: Industrial Service v Charles Ransford: fixed price or extra tanker loads for CCA plant cleansing
key_facts: Charles Ransford quoted a fixed £4,845 to steam-clean timber treatment tanks and remove Celcure contaminated waste from Industrial Service's plant.
Walters' confirmation letter referred to clearing holding tanks and removing arising sludge and 3% residual liquid; the parties misunderstood whether unused CCA solution remained in the tanks.
Nine tanker loads removed over 200,000 litres rather than the one part-load Rawlins had priced; extra charges were invoiced and Walters queried amounts without denying liability.
The judge found the fixed price covered only cleansing waste and small residues, not full unused liquid, and that extra work was agreed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a county court trial on payment for tank cleansing and hazardous waste removal at a timber treatment plant.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; respondents entitled to payment beyond the fixed quotation for additional tanker loads.
enrichment.ratio: On the true construction of the quotation and confirmation letter, the fixed price was not for removal of an indeterminate quantity of unused liquid in the tanks; post-contract correspondence showed acceptance that extra tanker loads would be paid for.
legal_issues: Whether the contract was a lump sum for all liquid in the tanks regardless of volume
Meaning of '3% residual liquid' as concentration versus quantity
Whether there was a contractual variation or agreement to pay for extra work
Whether mutual misunderstanding rendered the contract void

confidence.notes: Findings of fact are accepted on appeal and contractual construction reasoning is detailed.

notes: POCA s 328 account freeze application refused; statutory scheme and suspicion standard explained.

enrichment.short_title: Squirrell v Natwest: bank account freeze under Proceeds of Crime Act 2002
key_facts: Natwest froze Squirrell Ltd's account containing nearly £200,000 without explanation after forming a suspicion under POCA.
HM Customs and Excise intervened; the company sought unfreezing and disclosure of reasons for the block.
The bank acted under section 328 after an authorised disclosure; HMCE refused consent within the seven working-day moratorium.
No allegation was made that Squirrell or its funds were criminal property; the dispute concerned statutory constraints on operating the account.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery application for orders unfreezing a corporate bank account and requiring disclosure of the reasons for the freeze.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; the court could not order Natwest to operate the account or disclose reasons where POCA prohibited doing so.
enrichment.ratio: Where a bank reasonably suspects criminal property, section 328 prevents it facilitating transactions until appropriate consent is given or moratorium periods expire; the court cannot require conduct that would constitute a criminal offence under the statutory scheme.
legal_issues: Meaning of criminal property and relevant suspicion under sections 328 and 340
Whether the court could order the bank to unblock the account
Effect of anti-tip-off provisions on disclosure to the customer
Whether HMCE refused consent within the seven working-day period
linked_authorities: Hussien v Chong Fook Kam [1970] AC 942

confidence.notes: Statutory analysis and refusal of relief are clearly reasoned though underlying criminal allegations were not tried.

notes: Service out on Indian publisher refused to be set aside; copyright licensing and assignment issues arguable.

enrichment.short_title: Pearson v Prentice Hall India: service out on copyright licence termination dispute
key_facts: Pearson claimed Prentice Hall of India breached 97 low-cost reprint licence agreements by failing to pay royalties since 1996 and continuing to print after rights reverted.
Default notices were served in late 2003 and proceedings issued in England after permission to serve out in India.
The defendant challenged title to sue, the validity of termination under clause 7, and argued India was the appropriate forum given parallel proceedings there.
The agreements contained an English law clause but no jurisdiction clause; outstanding royalties were modest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Part 11 application to set aside permission to serve proceedings out of the jurisdiction and for a stay on forum non conveniens grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; permission to serve out upheld, stay refused, and permission granted to amend particulars of claim.
enrichment.ratio: At the jurisdiction stage the claimant showed reasonable prospects on complex assignment, notice and copyright-owner capacity issues; England was clearly the appropriate forum for English-law termination and account claims despite separate Indian proceedings between different parties.
legal_issues: Whether Pearson had title to sue and could validly serve default notices under clause 7
Effect of equitable versus legal assignment and section 136 notice requirements
Whether copyright assignment by writing made Pearson the licensor without notice to the licensee
Whether India was clearly the more appropriate forum
linked_authorities: Spiliada Maritime Corp v Cansulex Ltd [1987] AC 460
Warner Bros Records Inc v Rollgreen Ltd [1976] 1 QB 430
Three Rivers District Council v Bank of England [1996] QB 292

confidence.notes: Interlocutory jurisdiction ruling with detailed but non-final treatment of merits.

notes: Permission granted to appeal JR refusal alongside Part 7 procurement claim; Alcatel remedy gap argued.

enrichment.short_title: Cookson & Clegg v MoD: permission to appeal parallel procurement and judicial review claims
key_facts: Cookson & Clegg, a long-standing military clothing supplier, challenged the MoD's award of a call-off contract worth over £50 million to Cooneen Watts & Stone, a joint venture not on the shortlist.
Part 7 proceedings alleged breaches of the Public Supply Contracts Regulations; parallel judicial review was refused by Bennett J.
The claimant argued damages might be inadequate and that judicial review could provide remedies such as setting aside the contract unavailable in the Part 7 claim.
Trial of the Part 7 claim was listed for October 2005.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal Bennett J's refusal of permission for judicial review, with Part 7 proceedings continuing.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal to be heard by three judges with a half-day estimate.
enrichment.ratio: Despite Sedley LJ's view that Bennett J's discretionary refusal disclosed no error, there was sufficient prospect that the Full Court might hold judicial review could provide distinct public law remedies, including possible contract-setting-aside relief after Alcatel, to warrant permission.
legal_issues: Whether judicial review adds remedies beyond Part 7 damages for procurement breaches
Whether the Regulations are coextensive with public law rights
Adequacy of damages for loss of a call-off contract
Whether parallel JR and Part 7 proceedings should be consolidated
linked_authorities: Commission of the European Communities v Siemens AG (Case C-337/98) [1999] ECR I-7671

confidence.notes: Permission-only ruling; underlying procurement merits undetermined.

notes: Family company share transfer trial; torn stock transfer form held incomplete; rectification ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Smith v Charles Building Services: validity of torn share transfer between brothers
key_facts: Steve and Terry Smith were registered as equal shareholders in Charles Building Services Ltd, a building company spun off from their family painting business.
In 1997 Terry procured Steve to sign a stock transfer form for his one share; Steve tore it up after dividend negotiations failed.
Terry reconstituted the torn form with sellotape, backdated it, and registered himself as sole shareholder; further share allotments followed.
Steve claimed he was always intended to have an interest and that the transfer was never completed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Chancery trial claim for rectification of the company share register to restore the claimant's shareholding.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the 1997 transfer was not completed and the register should be rectified to restore Steve's share.
enrichment.ratio: Steve was intended to hold a share in CBS as part of a joint venture supported by the family company; he signed the transfer conditionally without handing it over, so execution was incomplete and subsequent registration was invalid.
legal_issues: Whether Steve was intended to be a shareholder in CBS at incorporation
Whether signing without delivery completed an effective share transfer
Effect of tearing up a signed but undated stock transfer form
Whether rectification should restore a 50% or reduced moral entitlement

confidence.notes: Detailed findings of fact and clear final rectification conclusion.

notes: AG reference: 'immigrant doctor' capable of racial aggravation; judge wrongly withdrew case from jury.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference No 4 of 2004: 'immigrant' as racially aggravated assault
key_facts: Mrs D was charged with racially aggravated assault after calling Dr N an 'immigrant doctor' and assaulting him at his surgery.
The trial judge directed acquittal at the close of the prosecution case, holding 'immigrant' was too vague to denote a racial group.
Dr N was of Asian origin; the prosecution case was that the epithet demonstrated hostility based on race, colour, nationality or national origins.
The Attorney General referred the point of law under section 36 of the 1972 Act.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1972 following directed acquittal on a racially aggravated assault charge.
enrichment.outcome: Court held the judge erred; use of 'immigrant doctor' was capable of demonstrating hostility within section 28 and should have been left to the jury.
enrichment.ratio: A racial group may be defined non-inclusively by reference to nationality or national origins; calling a victim an 'immigrant doctor' can, in context, demonstrate hostility based on perceived non-British membership of a racial group, following Orpheanos and DPP v M.
legal_issues: Whether 'immigrant' denotes a specific racial group under section 28(4)
Whether non-Britishness suffices as a racial group definition
Distinction between construction of the word and factual demonstration of hostility
Application of Orpheanos and DPP v M (A Minor) to pejorative non-inclusive terms
linked_authorities: Orpheanos v Queen Mary College [1985] AC 761

confidence.notes: Statutory construction opinion clearly stated; underlying assault facts not retried.

notes: Costs undertaking under interim receiver order; 9 August disclosure order held fresh so undertaking did not bite.

enrichment.short_title: Rio Properties v Gibson Dunn: costs undertaking and bankruptcy disclosure orders
key_facts: Rio Properties obtained bankruptcy and interim receiver orders against Amer Almidani over gambling debts, with disclosure orders against Gibson Dunn as solicitors administering his father's estate.
Rio gave an undertaking in the July 2002 receiver order to pay reasonable costs of third parties complying with that order.
After Buchler became trustee on 7 August 2002, a further disclosure order was made on 9 August; Gibsons incurred compliance costs.
HHJ Maddocks ordered Rio to pay Gibsons' costs under the undertaking; this court held the 9 August order was a fresh trustee order outside the undertaking.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from an order requiring the petitioning creditor to pay solicitors' costs under an undertaking given in interim receiver proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; paragraph 1 of the 16 December 2004 costs order set aside; judge's refusal to apply CPR 36 to a costs settlement offer upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Once the receivership ended on appointment of the trustee, the 9 August disclosure order was substantively a new order by the trustee, not compliance with the July 2002 receiver order; costs incurred under it did not fall within Rio's undertaking.
legal_issues: Scope of an undertaking to pay third-party costs of complying with an interim receiver order
Whether the 9 August disclosure order continued the receiver regime or was a fresh trustee order
Whether CPR 36 principles apply to offers to settle outstanding costs claims
Discretion to mark rejection of a composite costs settlement offer
linked_authorities: Rio Properties Inc v Gibson Dunn & Crutcher [2004] 1 WLR 2702

confidence.notes: Prior Court of Appeal judgment provides factual background; costs analysis is explicit.

notes: RIPA intrusive surveillance: Surveillance Commissioner approval conclusive; no fishing disclosure of authorisations.

enrichment.short_title: R v GS: disclosure of RIPA intrusive surveillance authorisations
key_facts: Nine defendants facing drug conspiracy trial sought exclusion of covert home recordings obtained under RIPA Part II intrusive surveillance authorisations.
At a section 30 preparatory hearing the judge admitted the evidence subject to prosecution disclosure review but refused defence access to underlying authorisation material.
The prosecution relied on Surveillance Commissioners' approval forms and section 91(10) ouster; defence sought material to mount a section 78 fairness application.
No specific irregularity was identified; the request was described as a fishing expedition.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal under section 35 of the 1996 Act against rulings on admissibility and non-disclosure of intrusive surveillance authorisation material.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals dismissed; Surveillance Commissioner approvals suffice to establish lawfulness and defence is not entitled to underlying authorisation documents absent a borderline H & C disclosure case.
enrichment.ratio: Section 91(10) and section 27 RIPA make approved authorisations lawful for all purposes and not open to relitigation in criminal proceedings; section 78 fairness does not permit fishing disclosure of authorisation material, though prosecution must discharge normal unused material duties under R v H & C.
legal_issues: Whether Surveillance Commissioners' approvals conclusively establish lawfulness of intrusive surveillance
Whether defence are entitled to underlying authorisation material for section 78 applications
Relationship between RIPA lawfulness and PACE section 78 admissibility
Application of R v H & C to covert surveillance material

confidence.notes: Appellate ruling on procedure and disclosure is comprehensive; trial not yet concluded at hearing.

notes: Warehouse insurance forum battle; anti-suit injunction granted after submission to English jurisdiction.

enrichment.short_title: CNA v Office Depot: anti-suit injunction after warehouse insurance forum agreement
key_facts: Insurers and Office Depot group companies disputed coverage for unequal settlement of an Oldham warehouse insured under English local policies and Florida-governed DIC policies.
The defendants initially submitted to English jurisdiction, withdrew Part 11 challenges, and agreed in June 2004 to stay Florida proceedings pending resolution in the Commercial Court.
After failed settlement talks, OD Inc commenced fresh proceedings in the Florida Federal Court on period 5 DIC policies alone and sought to stay the English action.
Substantial costs and expert evidence had been incurred in England over nearly two years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications for an anti-suit injunction restraining Florida proceedings and for a stay of the consolidated English insurance action.
enrichment.outcome: Stay application refused; anti-suit injunction granted to restrain the Florida Federal Court action as a breach of the June 2004 agreement and unconscionable given submission to jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Having submitted to English jurisdiction, agreed Florida proceedings would follow English determination, and incurred substantial costs here, it is unconscionable and a breach of contract to commence parallel Federal proceedings; England remains the proper forum even for Florida-law DIC claims tied to the Oldham warehouse.
legal_issues: Whether the June 2004 agreement precluded fresh Florida proceedings
Whether a late stay application after submission to jurisdiction should be granted
Whether Owusu prevents staying claims against the English company ODUK
When anti-suit relief is appropriate for breach of forum agreement
linked_authorities: Reichhold Norway ASA v Goldman Sachs [2000] 1 WLR 173

confidence.notes: Procedural history and final injunctive relief are clearly recorded.
